common_name: Natal Lily (Parrot Gladiolus, Dragon's Head Gladiolus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep after soil has warmed following the last frost, in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Natal lily is a summer-rainfall South African species considerably hardier than most gladiolus and, unlike tender hybrid gladiolus, can often overwinter in the ground in zone 7 with a heavy mulch.

directions: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun once the soil has warmed in spring; Natal lily tolerates summer humidity and rainfall far better than the Cape winter-rainfall gladiolus species, making it one of the easiest species gladioli for Gulf South gardens. Gladiolus dalenii carries up to five branching spikes of hooded, orange-scarlet to yellow-throated flowers in late summer and early fall, and is a principal wild ancestor of the modern hybrid garden gladiolus, contributing much of the vigor and color range seen in today's cultivars. It multiplies steadily by cormlets and, in zones 8-10, can be left undisturbed in the ground year-round; farther north the corms are best lifted and stored after foliage yellows in fall. The nodding, hooded flower form and reliable perennial habit make it a valuable back-of-border plant for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Italian gladiolus is a fully hardy, fall-planted, spring-blooming species that naturalizes readily in dry, sunny sites and does not need lifting in zones 7-10.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Italian gladiolus, like its close relative Byzantine gladiolus, is planted in autumn and blooms in late spring rather than following the tender-summer-gladiolus schedule most gardeners expect. Gladiolus italicus produces loose, one-sided spikes of up to twenty small, pinkish-purple flowers on wiry stems in May and June, and has long grown as a cornfield weed across the Mediterranean basin, where it is sometimes still called corn flag for its habit of springing up among grain crops. It is drought-tolerant once established and multiplies by offset cormlets to form informal drifts in gravelly or sandy, alkaline-leaning soils. Bees and other pollinators visit the flowers readily, and the plant combines well with other fall-planted hardy bulbs such as Byzantine gladiolus and species tulips in naturalistic, low-water spring plantings.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Painted Lady gladiolus is a winter-growing, summer-dormant Cape species that produces its soft pink, dark-marked flowers in late spring, following the same reverse growth cycle as other winter-rainfall South African bulbs.

directions: Plant corms in fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and allow the foliage to die back naturally in early summer without supplemental water; Painted Lady gladiolus follows the winter-growing, summer-dormant cycle typical of Cape winter-rainfall bulbs, so it needs to stay dry and undisturbed through the hot months. Gladiolus carneus bears loose, one-sided spikes of three to twelve softly funnel-shaped, pale pink to cream flowers marked with deep carmine feathering on the lower petals, blooming for up to a month in late spring. It is native to sandstone and clay slopes of the Western Cape and performs best in zones 8-10 where winters stay mild and wet while summers turn dry, making it a good companion for other Cape bulbs like Sparaxis and Babiana in a Mediterranean-style bulb border. Where summer irrigation cannot be avoided, grow it in containers that can be kept dry and dormant through summer.

subcategory: Texas/Gulf Coast native monarch host plant

planting.note: Direct sow in spring (cold stratify 3-4 weeks first) or set out container plants in lean, well-drained, often caliche or limestone-derived soil in full sun; zizotes milkweed is deeply taprooted and resents transplanting once established, so choose a permanent site.

directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, often rocky or caliche soil in full sun, or set out young container-grown plants before the root becomes pot-bound; zizotes milkweed develops a deep taproot early and transplants poorly once mature. Asclepias oenotheroides is a low, sprawling milkweed native to the dry prairies, roadsides, and open brushland of Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, where it blooms over an unusually long season, from spring through fall in the Gulf South, producing small greenish-white to cream flower clusters held close to the stem. It serves as a larval host plant for monarch and queen butterflies and is especially valuable in hot, dry, low-rainfall gardens where showier milkweed species struggle. Its low, spreading form suits the front of a native wildflower border or a xeric pollinator planting, and once established it needs no supplemental irrigation beyond occasional deep watering during extended drought.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; in zones 8-10 corms can also be planted in fall for larger plants and earlier bloom, and are typically left in the ground year-round.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; scarlet freesia performs best with consistent moisture during active growth and appreciates a light, dappled-shade site along the edge of a woodland border or beneath open shrubs. Freesia laxa (long sold under the names Anomatheca laxa and Lapeirousia laxa) is a South African corm with grassy, iris-like foliage and loose sprays of small, bright scarlet-red, white-throated flowers marked with dark carmine blotches, blooming from late spring into summer. Where hardy, it self-sows and multiplies by offset corms to form spreading, low-maintenance colonies that return reliably each year without becoming aggressive. A white-flowered form and the pale pink 'Joan Evans' selection are sometimes offered alongside the classic scarlet species, and all combine nicely with ferns, hostas, and other light-shade perennials in Gulf South and coastal Southeast gardens.

common_name: Millenium Ornamental Onion (2018 Perennial Plant of the Year)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring (or fall in mild climates) in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Millenium is a sterile hybrid that forms tight, glossy clumps and needs division only when clumps become crowded after several years.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Millenium ornamental onion tolerates heat, humidity, and short dry spells better than most ornamental alliums, which is part of why it was named the Perennial Plant Association's 2018 Perennial Plant of the Year. It forms a tidy, deer- and rabbit-resistant mound of glossy, strap-like foliage topped from midsummer into early fall by two-inch, rose-purple globe flowers that draw heavy traffic from bees, butterflies, and other pollinators for weeks on end. Unlike many ornamental onions, this hybrid is sterile and does not set seed, so it stays in a neat, non-spreading clump rather than self-sowing through the garden. It holds up well in the humid Gulf South as long as drainage is good, and pairs nicely with coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, and ornamental grasses in a late-summer pollinator border.

planting.note: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, alkaline (limestone or chalk-derived) soil in full sun after the last frost; Leavenworth's eryngo germinates somewhat erratically and benefits from light raking-in rather than deep burial, and self-sows freely once established.

directions: Direct sow in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; Leavenworth's eryngo thrives in the same dry, rocky, limestone or chalk prairie conditions where most garden flowers struggle, and needs no supplemental fertility. This branching annual in the carrot family is grown not for its small, inconspicuous true flowers but for the intensely violet-purple, spiny bracts that surround each dense flower head, turning the whole upper plant a vivid, almost electric magenta-purple from midsummer through fall. It is native to dry prairies, glades, and roadsides from Missouri and Kansas south through Oklahoma and Texas, and is a magnet for an extraordinary range of pollinators, including bumblebees, native bees, wasps, beetles, and clouds of migrating butterflies drawn to the abundant nectar. Cut stems dry well and hold their purple color, making it a favorite for dried arrangements as well as the pollinator border. Allow seed heads to mature and drop for reliable self-sown returns the following year.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; western ironweed spreads by rhizomes once established, so give it room or plant it where a colonizing habit is welcome, such as a large native meadow planting.

directions: Plant in average to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; western ironweed is adaptable to poor, dry, or occasionally clay soils and needs no irrigation once established. Vernonia baldwinii is a coarse, upright prairie perennial native from Texas and Louisiana north through the central Plains to Nebraska and Iowa, producing broad, flat-topped clusters of vivid red-violet, thistle-like flower heads from midsummer through fall that are heavily worked by monarchs, swallowtails, skippers, and native bees during a season when many other prairie flowers have finished blooming. It spreads by rhizomes to form expanding colonies over time, so it is best suited to naturalized meadow plantings, roadsides, or large borders rather than small, tidy beds. The tough, deep-rooted plants tolerate heat, drought, and occasional mowing better than most late-season pollinator perennials, and the dried seed heads provide texture and food for birds into winter.
